sweep_summary: Herero (here1253) is in the catalog as tonal, deciding source Elderkin 2003 (Nurse & Philippson ch. 29, full text held by the project, no stress statement). this search of works with stress in the title's single title item, Möhlig 2003 'The prosodological structure of Herero' (FAB 15: 165-180), is a first-hand modern prosodic study; no open copy exists (archive.org 0 hits, HathiTrust search blocked, no DOI), but Google Books snippet view (12 feed queries saved) yields the key passage of sec. 2.2.2 'Respiratory accent': a primary and a secondary accent exist and 'Words usually bear a main accent on the penultimate syllable' (okuMUna 'to see', omuRIse 'herdsman', oMUre 'tall'), with accent shift onto following demonstratives (okakàMBÈ ngà) and in predicative clauses, and an expressive first-syllable accent that demotes the penultimate demarcation accent to secondary. This refines the catalog (which says no modern source states word stress) and points to reclassification tonal -> fixed penultimate-with-tone under the catalog's Bantu convention, but the full text (Möhlig 2003, or Möhlig & Kavari 2008 Reference Grammar pp. 40-79, publisher-PDF only, no preview, not in HathiTrust) should be read first — both priority high. Also re-downloaded from the migrated AAeO host the open-access Lusekelo 2009 review of Möhlig & Kavari 2008 (silent on stress, tone only) and re-read Brincker 1886 (root-syllable accent, 19th c.). Google Books HTML and HathiTrust could not be reached by automated download/JS challenge; archive.org's 2002 sketch is lending-restricted. written under

Words usually bear a main accent on the penultimate syllable, for instance: o.ku."múná o.mu."risè o.mu."hòngè 'to see' o."mu.rè 'tall in cl 1' 'herdsman ... syllable of the noun, thus: o.ka.kà"mbè ngà. This shift shows that, despite of being written disjunctively in the ruling orthography, the demonstratives are ... shift of accent can also be observed in so-called predicative clauses ... first syllable degrading the demarcation accent to a secondary rank.

new_statements.locator: sec. 2.2.2 'Respiratory accent' (pp. 165-180; Google Books snippet view, page number not shown)
new_statements.reading: The one modern first-hand prosodic study of Herero states a word-level dynamic ('respiratory') accent that usually falls on the penultimate syllable, co-existing with lexical/grammatical H/L tone; there is also a secondary accent, the accent shifts rightward onto a following demonstrative (noun + demonstrative form one accentual word) and in predicative clauses, and an expressive first-syllable accent can demote the penultimate 'demarcation accent' to secondary. This directly fills the catalog's stated gap ('no word-stress rule stated in any reachable modern source') and, under the catalog's convention for penult-stress-plus-tone Bantu languages (Shona, Setswana, Sotho, Lingala), argues for reclassification tonal -> fixed penultimate (dominant, 'usually') with tone kept in the tone note. Evidence is snippet-only: 12 Google Books feed snippets (verbatim, no page numbers) — the full text of Möhlig 2003 or of Möhlig & Kavari 2008 pp. 40-79 should be read before a final reclassify.

Gesetze über die Betonung sind noch nicht gefunden, und man muß sich die Betonung deshalb von Eingebornen vorsprechen lassen. u vor einem Vokal klingt in der Regel wie engl. w, z. B. in water. new_statements.translation: ... Laws governing the accentuation have not yet been found, and one must therefore have the accentuation pronounced to one by natives. u before a vowel as a rule sounds like English w, e.g. in water. In the accentuation one must take care, e.g. ómbua 'dog', not ombúa. In the printed texts oa is often written instead of ua and y is found instead of j. When using the literature one should get used to these fluctuations of spelling.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Meinhof states that no laws of accentuation (Betonung) had been found for Herero; placement must be learned word by word from native speakers. His one example, ómbua 'dog' with the accent on the first syllable (o-mbu-a) and explicitly not on the penult (ombúa), shows that he did not take the accent to be penultimate. The feed's search for Tonhöhe, Töne, hohen/tiefen Ton, Tonzeichen, Akut, Druck, betont, Stammsilbe, letzte Silbe within the 1909 volumes returned no hits, so the 1909 grammar appears to contain no separate tone chapter; his 'Betonung' with an acute may well be the H tone of ómbwa heard as prominence, so this is not a clean stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the source says the rules are not yet discovered. The snippet begins mid-sentence ('.. Gesetze über die Betonung'), so the sentence's first word(s) are not visible.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Otjiherero of Namibia (German South West Africa in 1909); no dialect is singled out in the snippets read. The Google Books volume 1LsxAQAAMAAJ (WISC, 1973) is a reprint bundle of the 'Deutsche Kolonialsprachen' series and also contains Duala and Swahili text (snippets about Tiefton/Hochton, ndamba, mzee), so its tone snippets were not attributed to Herero.

readall_conflicts: Meinhof 1909 (snippet, same Princeton copy as the HathiTrust item) says that laws of accentuation for Herero had not been found and must be learned from native speakers, and gives ómbua 'dog' with the accent on the first syllable, explicitly 'not ombúa'. The catalog's existing statement from Möhlig 2003 (also snippet-only, sec. 2.2.2 'Respiratory accent') says words usually bear a main accent on the penultimate syllable, alongside lexical/grammatical H/L tone. The two disagree on placement for the one Meinhof example and on whether a rule exists at all; the likeliest resolution is that Meinhof's 1909 'Betonung' (acute) records the high tone he heard as prominence (his volume shows no tone chapter and no hits for Tonhöhe/Töne/Tonzeichen), whereas Möhlig separates tone from a dynamic penult accent. The 2002 sketch (Möhlig, Marten & Kavari), which would arbitrate, is lending-restricted on archive.org and could not be read.

sources.quote: 7) a) Der Accent eilt nur in affektierter Rede zur letzten Silbe zum Ende des Satzes hin; in gewöhnlicher Rede kann man denselben nur auf die Grundsilbe eines Wortes legen, wodurch letztere als solche sich kennzeichnet, wie ú-nga-ra, longa, arbeite; Nomen: oma-ú-nga-ri-ro, ovi-úngura, oma-lóngelo ... b) Wörter, in denen sich ka ... befindet, haben den Accent auf dem ka [Translation: The accent moves to the last syllable, toward the end of the sentence, only in affected speech; in ordinary speech it can be placed only on the root syllable of a word, which thereby marks it as such ... b) words containing ka ... carry the accent on the ka]
sources.locator: grammar appendix sec. XVIII item 7a-b ( lines 30991-31000)
sources.note: 19th-century missionary statement: word accent on the root syllable (first stem syllable), final accent only in affected/emphatic speech; agrees with Viehe 1897 (root syllable) and against Kolbe 1883 (generally final). Impressionistic, pre-tonological; not a modern source.

sources.citation: Lusekelo, Amani. 2009. Möhlig & Kavari 2008. Reference Grammar of Herero (Otjiherero) [review]. Afrikanistik-Aegyptologie-Online 2009. doi 10.18716/ojs/aaeo/2009_3535.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: The bank of tonemic behaviours in Otjiherero is intensively provided (pp. 40-79). Such behaviours range from distinctive tone patterns, examples the lexical tones H-H -hórá „to ripen‟, H-L -hóra „to remove hair‟ and L-L -hora „be stiff‟ (p.41) to an extra high tone occurring in the language, exemplified by o.mbwá „dog‟ and Ő.mbwá 'it is a dog‟ (p. 45). Moreover, the introduction of pragmatics and language use through intonation and focus into contemporary Bantu grammars by the authors is highly recommendable (pp. 47-50).
sources.note: The review (already the catalog's supporting source) reports only the tone analysis, extra-high tone, intonation and focus of Möhlig & Kavari 2008; it never mentions stress or accent placement, so it is silent on where word accent falls. Re-downloaded from the migrated OJS host (same 7-page PDF).
